title: Reading User Input ⌨️
description: Make interactive scripts with the `read` command – ask questions and capture answers.

slides.title: The `read` Command 📥
slides.content:
## Talk to Your User

`read` pauses the script and waits for the user to type something (and press Enter). It stores the input in a variable.

Syntax: `read variable_name`

You can read multiple values: `read first last` splits the input on spaces.

Often combined with `-p` to show a prompt: `read -p "Enter name: " username`.

slides.title: Simple read
slides.content: Ask for a name and greet:

quizData.question: Which `read` option shows a prompt message?
quizData.explanation: `-p` allows you to display a prompt string before reading input.

slides.title: Silent Input with -s 🤫
slides.content:
## Reading Passwords

`-s` (silent) hides the user's typing – perfect for passwords.

```bash
read -sp "Password: " pass
echo  # new line
echo "Password set."
```
No characters are echoed back.

slides.title: Secret Mode
slides.codeSnippet:
read -sp "Enter secret: " secret
echo
echo "Your secret is $secret"

quizData.question: The `-s` flag makes `read` ignore spaces in input.
quizData.explanation: `-s` suppresses echoing, making input silent. It does not affect whitespace handling.

slides.title: Reading Multiple Variables 🎯
slides.content:
## Splitting Input

If you give `read` several variable names, the input is split by spaces (or characters in `$IFS`) and assigned in order.

```bash
read first last
echo "First: $first, Last: $last"
```
If there are more words than variables, the last variable gets the remainder.

You can also read into an **array** (later chapter) with `-a`.

slides.title: Multi‑word Input
slides.codeSnippet:
echo "Enter full name:"
read first last
echo "Hello, $first $last!"

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Timeout Input
Use `-t seconds` to limit waiting. If the user doesn't respond in time, `read` returns an error (exit code >0).
